title: Hundreds evacuate Oleshky under Melania Trump-brokered ceasefire | CNN
text:
Source: CNN

Hundreds of people from an occupied town in southern Ukraine who survived months without basic supplies were evacuated on Friday under a ceasefire agreement negotiated byfirst lady Melania Trump.

“In just a few hours, all Ukrainian citizens evacuated from Oleshky, along with the Ukrainian delegation, will be on Ukrainian soil,” Ukrainian parliamentarian Davyd Arakhamia said on Telegram after announcing that the fourth and final plane carrying the evacuees landed in Gomel, Belarus, on Saturday.

The town of Oleshky in the southern Ukrainian region of Kherson has been under continuous Russian occupation since April 2022. Some 2,000 people, including 50 children, have been stuck in the heavily destroyed city, Ukrainian authorities say.

All access routes were either heavily mined or swarming with drones, making an escape impossible – until the intervention from Trump helped to make the evacuations possible.

Here is what we know.

Teams of humanitarian workers and officials from both Russia and Ukraine were in Oleshky on Friday, accompanying those who wanted to leave and providing much-needed humanitarian help to people who chose to stay.

The temporary truce that has made the evacuation possible went into effect on Tuesday and has since expanded across the Kherson region. The ceasefire has also brought relief to Kherson, the Ukraine-controlled capital of the region, which has been under near-constant drone attacks from Russia.

Ukraine’s ombudsman Dmytro Lubinets traveled to Oleshky to personally escort the evacuees into Ukraine-controlled territory, becoming the first high-profile Ukrainian official to openly travel to occupied areas under Russian control and Russia since the start of the war.

The evacuation began on Friday afternoon local time. According to Lubinets, 25 buses with the capacity of 750 seats were part of the operation.

Access routes to Oleshky have been heavily mined and littered with drone and vehicle debris, making them virtually impassable. A demining operation began on Tuesday after the ceasefire came into effect, with both Russia and Ukraine announcing its completion on Thursday. Two people participating in the clearing operation were killed, according to the authorities.

Evacuation across the Dnipro River directly into Ukraine-controlled territory is not possible. According to Arakhamia, the group traveled through the occupied Ukrainian peninsula of Crimea to Anapa in Russia’s Krasnodar region.

The evacuees then flew from Anapa airport to Gomel, Belarus, according to the Russian Defense Ministry and Ukrainian officials.

The evacuees are expected to arrive at the Ukrainian border by bus later on Saturday, where medical teams were waiting to assess them.

“We’re waiting for people,” said Andriy Zhydenko, director general of the Chernihiv Regional Hospital. “There are people with injuries, stroke survivors, and those with limited mobility.”

Those whose lives are not in immediate danger will be transported directly to Kyiv, Zhydenko told CNN, adding that the evacuees would need to be fed very carefully because they had been starving.

“For us, this day is a celebration – we are bringing our citizens home,” he said. “All of my staff wanted to come here.”

The humanitarian situation has deteriorated in recent months. The town was reported by Ukrainian authorities to have ran out of food and other supplies in September, with no access to electricity, gas, medicine and other essentials.

“We ourselves are already exhausted. It’s very hard,” a woman in Oleshky who chose to remain anonymous told Ukrainian television. “Constantly in the dark. If we were in good health, maybe we would have stayed longer, but now that’s it. We want to be with our children.”

“People in temporarily occupied Oleshky are starving. There is almost nothing left to eat. Reports indicate that civilians are being forced to survive on grass and weeds, while medicines, clean water, electricity and medical care are increasingly out of reach. Children are trapped in these conditions too,” Andrii Sybiha, Ukraine’s foreign minister, said earlier this month.

The town was flooded when the Nova Kakhovka Dam collapsed in 2023. Several hundred people were reported to have died in the flooding. Evidence has pointed to Russia being responsible for an explosion that destroyed the dam, a charge Moscow has denied.

Further destruction came in the subsequent years of heavy fighting in the area.

Some 40% of the town’s prewar population of around 24,000 managed to flee to Ukraine-controlled territory when it was still possible early in the fighting, according to the Institute for the Study of War (ISW), a US-based conflict observer. Thousands of others have escaped since then, but many remained, either unable or unwilling to leave.

The town plays an important part in Russia’s military operations in the region. It sits near the banks of the Dnipro River, directly opposite Ukrainian positions along the front line of the war.

As the two sides fire at each other, the people in Oleshky are caught in the middle.

All escape routes toward Ukraine gradually disappeared as the Russian occupation intensified.

And while it had previously been possible to flee the city by going deeper into Russia-controlled territory, this has also become impossible in recent months, as fighting intensified and all routes out were either mined or swarming with drones.

Kyiv has made at least three attempts earlier this year to get Russia to allow evacuations into Ukraine, but Moscow has always rejected them.

“It is important that Kherson has found this much-needed calm,” Ukraine’s President Volodymyr Zelensky said in his nightly address on Friday. “Russia must end this war of its own making.”

The exact number of people who are being evacuated has not been announced by neither Russian nor Ukrainian authorities, but it is clear that some people have decided to stay.

One woman — who did not give her name — told Ukrainian television that while she would love to leave, she cannot fly on a plane and will be staying in Oleshky with her husband.

Some older residents have been unwilling to leave their homes despite the dire humanitarian and security situation. For many, this is exacerbated by the fact that they cannot take their animals with them.

Videos shared by Lubinets’ office shows the ombudsman greeting groups of emotional residents in Oleshky, discussing their journey. In one, he is seen talking to people leaving about those who want to stay, telling them, “I was told that it’s their own choice. We will at least make sure that at least some humanitarian aid comes.”

This is a major worry for Ukrainian forces. The ceasefire set to expire on Sunday.

The ISW said in a report on Oleshky that the Russian military has embedded itself in Oleshky, using the town as a key forward position in the region.

Ukraine has been attacking the area with drones as it tries to disrupt Russian supply lines – but this has also impacted the civilians still left in the city.

Lubinets said last week that while Ukraine has been working to resolve the humanitarian crisis in Oleshky since late February, “things really started moving in September — thanks to Melania Trump.”

Ukrainian officials have stepped up their efforts to raise alarm over the situation in Oleshky in September and testimonies from the town raised alarm around the world, with international organizations, faith leaders and others calling for urgent action.

When she first announced the ceasefire last Friday, the first lady said she worked directly with Ukrainian and Russian leadership as the “exclusive intermediary” and initiated discussions to secure the terms of the ceasefire agreement.

Trump has been previously involved in securing the return to Ukraine of several Ukrainian children who were taken to Russia after the war started.

While the ceasefire appeared to be holding on Friday, chances of it turning into a wider peace agreement between Russia and Ukraine are slim – despite renewed push for diplomatic solution by the Trump administration.

US President Donald Trump’s envoy Steve Witkoff has recently held a meeting with Zelensky in Norway before flying to St. Petersburg to meet with the Russian President Vladimir Putin, negotiating among others on the possibility of holding tri-lateral meetings in the future.

However, Putin has since reiterated his maximalist demands, including on territory and Ukraine’s sovereignty – red lines for Kyiv and its allies.

But while a wider peace agreement is unlikely for now, Ukrainian officials have expressed some hope that similar localized ceasefires could happen elsewhere along the front line to provide some relieve the long-suffering civilian population.

CNN’s Laura Sharman contributed to this report.

CNN’s Laura Sharman contributed to this report.
